title: Être and nationality
goal: Say your nationality with the verb être, and ask other people theirs.

drills.explain: Add -e for the feminine: français → française.

drills.prompt: Amira is Canadian. Which is right?
drills.explain: Amira is a woman → canadienne; elle → est.

blocks.title: A welcome evening for newcomers in Montréal
blocks.context: Camille, a volunteer, chats with Raj and Amira.

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Bonsoir ! Je suis Camille. Je suis québécoise.
lines.en: Good evening! I'm Camille. I'm from Québec.

lines.speaker: Raj
lines.fr: Enchanté, Camille. Moi, je suis Raj. Je suis indien.
lines.en: Nice to meet you, Camille. I'm Raj. I'm Indian.

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Et toi, Amira ? Tu es de quelle nationalité ?
lines.en: And you, Amira? What's your nationality?

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.fr: Je suis marocaine. Mais maintenant, je suis à Montréal !
lines.en: I'm Moroccan. But now I'm in Montréal!

lines.speaker: Raj
lines.fr: Nous sommes tous à Montréal maintenant.

blocks.body: Listen first. Try to understand before you tap a line to see the English.

blocks.title: Être means “to be”
blocks.body:
[[Être]] is the most common verb in French, and it is **irregular**: each form has to be learned. Use it to say who you are, your nationality, your job, and where you are right now.

For now, learn the six forms as sound chunks. Several are pronounced the same way.

blocks.title: Être in the present
head: être
English
rows: you are (formal, or more than one person)
blocks.note: [[es]] and [[est]] sound exactly the same: like the letter *é* in English “hay” without the *y*.

blocks.title: Saying your nationality
blocks.note: In French, nationality adjectives take **no capital letter** and **change for women**. Usually you add **-e**; words ending in **-ien** double the n: **-ienne**.

examples.fr: Je suis canadien. / Je suis canadienne.
Il est français. / Elle est française.
examples.en: He is French. / She is French.

examples.fr: Je suis indien. / Je suis indienne.

blocks.body:
The added **-e** is silent, but it makes the consonant before it **heard**:

- [[français]] ends in a vowel sound; [[française]] ends with a *z* sound.
- [[canadien]] ends in a nasal vowel; in [[canadienne]] you hear the *n*.
- [[chinois]] → [[chinoise]]: the *z* sound appears.

So listen for that final consonant: it tells you the speaker is talking about a woman.

- **Capital letters:** [[Je suis Canadien]] is wrong; write [[Je suis canadien]]. Capitals are used only for the *people* as nouns: [[les Canadiens]] (the Canadians).
- **Avoir instead of être:** English speakers sometimes say [[J'ai canadien]]. Nationality always uses **être**.
- **No article:** say [[Je suis français]], not [[Je suis un français]].

In Québec, many people describe themselves as [[québécois]] / [[québécoise]] rather than (or as well as) [[canadien]]. Both are normal; it is about identity as much as citizenship. You will also hear [[On est à Montréal]] for “we are in Montréal” — [[on]] is the everyday way to say *we*.

blocks.title: Listen and repeat
blocks.note: Repeat each line out loud, then record yourself and compare.

lines.tip: Now you hear the n at the end.

lines.en: Are you French? (formal, to a woman)

blocks.prompt: Who is the speaker talking about?
blocks.explain: [[chinoise]] — you hear the z sound, so it is feminine.
[[canadien]] ends in a nasal vowel, no n sound: masculine.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.intro: Answer without scrolling back. Getting something wrong now helps you remember it later.

blocks.prompt: Olivier is French. Which sentence is correct?
optionFeedback: française is the feminine form; Olivier is a man.
es goes with tu. With il/elle or a name, use est.
No capital letter for nationality adjectives.

blocks.explain: With nous, use sommes, and make the adjective plural: canadiens (or canadiennes for a group of women).

blocks.prompt: Match each form to its subject.

blocks.explain: Amira is a woman: marocain + e = marocaine.
Tu es de quelle nationalité ? is the friendly, spoken way to ask.

blocks.prompt: Introduce yourself at the welcome evening: say hello, your name, your nationality, and ask someone else theirs.
checklist: A question: Et toi ? / Tu es de quelle nationalité ?

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Bonsoir ! Je suis Mei. Je suis chinoise, et maintenant je suis à Vancouver. Et toi ? Tu es de quelle nationalité ?
models.en: Good evening! I'm Mei. I'm Chinese, and now I'm in Vancouver. And you? What's your nationality?

blocks.prompt: Write 3 short sentences: your nationality, the nationality of someone in your family, and a question for a new friend.
checklist: Use il est or elle est with the right ending

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Je suis indien. Ma femme est indienne aussi. Et toi, tu es de quelle nationalité ?
models.en: I'm Indian. My wife is Indian too. And you, what's your nationality?

summary:
- Conjugate **être** in the present: [[je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont]]
- Say your nationality with the right masculine or feminine ending
- Ask [[Tu es de quelle nationalité ?]] and [[Et toi ?]]
